prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A high school dropout who stole the identity of a missing South Carolina woman and used it to gain admission to two Ivy League colleges has been arrested, police said Sunday. Esther Reed, who allegedly used a missing woman's ID to get into colleges, was arrested by U.S. Marshals. A fugitive for more than a year, Esther Reed was arrested Saturday by U.S. Marshals in suburban Chicago, said Clark Brazier, a spokesman for the police department in Traveler's Rest, South Carolina. Reed is scheduled to have a bond hearing this week in Illinois. South Carolina authorities are seeking to extradite her on charges of aggravated identity theft and wire fraud. Reed assumed the identity of Brooke Henson, who was 20 years old when she disappeared more than eight years ago from Travelers Rest, investigators say. It's unclear how Reed obtained Henson's personal information, but Reed used Henson's identity to take the SAT and GED, and then applied to the schools, said Jon Campbell, a Travelers Rest Police Department investigator who spoke to CNN last year. Officials at Harvard University and Columbia University have acknowledged that a Brooke Henson was enrolled at their schools, but said privacy laws prevent them from discussing details. "There's a little relief that goes with [the news of Reed's arrest]," Brooke's aunt Lisa Henson told CNN Sunday. "But [Brooke] is still missing. I'd like to have some answers. I would love to see [Reed] and look her in the eye and say, 'You're a horrible person.' " Police say they're confident Reed was not involved in Henson's disappearance. Authorities believe Henson was killed by someone who knew her. However, no body has been found and no arrests have been made. Henson's family had heard nothing about their missing relative for years until the summer of 2006, when New York City authorities told police in Travelers Rest that they had found her, alive and well, in Manhattan. The police relayed that message to Henson's family. "I was jumping for joy," said Lisa Henson. "It was incredible." But the family's joy was short-lived when it was revealed that the woman found was actually Reed. An ex-boyfriend told CNN that Reed -- posing as Henson -- often bragged about being a world-class chess player who earned a living playing the game competitively. The man told CNN that he believed her until he challenged her to a game and beat her. Originally from the tiny town of Townsend, Montana, Reed had been reported missing by her family in 1999, around the same time that Henson disappeared. In high school in Montana, Reed earned poor grades. "Esther was the kind of kid who would have been invisible," her English teacher James Therriault said. "If you didn't take pains to notice her presence." E-mail to a friend . CNN's Gary Tuchman and Ashley Fantz contributed to this report.

U.S. Marshals arrested Reed on Saturday in the Chicago suburbs after she had spent more than a year as a fugitive, according to Clark Brazier, a spokesman for the police department in Travelers Rest, South Carolina. She is expected to appear at a bond hearing in Illinois this week. Authorities in South Carolina are seeking her extradition to face aggravated identity theft and wire fraud charges.

Investigators allege that Reed posed as Brooke Henson, who was 20 when she vanished from Travelers Rest more than eight years ago. How Reed acquired Henson’s personal details remains unknown. Jon Campbell, an investigator with the Travelers Rest Police Department, told CNN last year that Reed used Henson’s name to take the SAT and GED before applying to colleges.

Harvard and Columbia have confirmed that someone using the name Brooke Henson attended their institutions, although officials said privacy laws prohibit them from providing further information.

Brooke’s aunt, Lisa Henson, said Reed’s arrest brought some comfort but did not resolve the family’s larger loss.

“There’s a little relief that goes with [the news of Reed’s arrest],” she told CNN on Sunday. “But [Brooke] is still missing. I’d like to have some answers. I would love to see [Reed] and look her in the eye and say, ‘You’re a horrible person.’”

Police do not believe Reed played any role in Henson’s disappearance. Investigators suspect that Henson was killed by someone she knew, but her body has never been recovered and no one has been arrested.

For years, Henson’s relatives received no news about her whereabouts. Then, in the summer of 2006, authorities in New York City informed Travelers Rest police that Henson had supposedly been found alive and well in Manhattan. Local officers passed that information along to the family.

“I was jumping for joy,” Lisa Henson recalled. “It was incredible.”

The celebration ended quickly when officials determined that the woman they had located was Reed rather than Henson.

A former boyfriend told CNN that Reed, while presenting herself as Henson, frequently claimed to be an elite chess player who supported herself through competitive play. He said he accepted the story until he played against her and won.

Reed came from Townsend, a very small Montana community. Her own family reported her missing in 1999, at roughly the same time Henson disappeared. Reed received poor grades while attending high school in Montana.

Her former English teacher, James Therriault, described her as someone who could easily go unnoticed.

“Esther was the kind of kid who would have been invisible,” he said, “if you didn’t take pains to notice her presence.”

CNN’s Gary Tuchman and Ashley Fantz contributed to the report.

Investigators quickly determined that the student was not Henson.

The discovery transformed what initially appeared to be a possible breakthrough in a missing-person case into a wide-ranging identity-theft investigation. After learning that investigators were closing in, she disappeared, setting off a manhunt that lasted more than a year. The case received national attention, and Reed was placed on a federal most-wanted list as agents tracked her movements and aliases.

She was ultimately captured in February 2008 in the Chicago suburb of Tinley Park, Illinois. At the time, authorities said, she was again living under another name. A person who became suspicious of inconsistencies in Reed’s story helped lead investigators to her.

Reed later pleaded guilty in federal court to fraud and identity-theft charges. She was sentenced to more than four years in prison and ordered to pay restitution.

The case drew attention not only because Reed had penetrated two Ivy League institutions, but also because of the painstaking way she constructed her false personas.
